evidence_quote: By 2011, Apple had sold 100 million iPhones worldwide, and became the largest mobile phone vendor in the world by revenue, surpassing longtime leader Nokia.
prompt: A maker of personal computers and of a leading digital music player has never sold a phone. Phone makers are adding music players that could erode its player sales, and wireless carriers normally dictate handset design and software. Proposal (2007): launch a touchscreen phone with no physical keyboard, a full web browser, email and its music player built in, at a premium price, sold through a single carrier that agrees to let the company control hardware and software design and pays it a share of monthly service revenue, in return for several years of exclusivity. Risks raised: no phone-industry experience; a premium price for a phone without a keyboard in a market led by keyboard business phones; exclusivity limits initial reach; the first version has no third-party applications.

evidence_quote: According to an International Data Corporation (IDC) study from March 2011, sales for all e-book readers worldwide reached 12.8 million in 2010; 48% of them were Kindles.
prompt: An online bookseller with a very large catalog wants to enter electronic books. Earlier dedicated e-readers sold poorly, publishers fear piracy, and the company has never designed consumer hardware. Proposal (2007): design and sell its own e-reader with a paper-like screen and a free built-in cellular connection, so a buyer can browse and download books from the company's store without a computer, with new releases at a single low price per title. Risks raised: hardware is outside the company's experience; low e-book prices may squeeze margins and annoy publishers; earlier e-readers found few buyers; the device may cannibalize print sales.

evidence_quote: As of 2013, the service was the largest PC game distribution platform with an estimated 75% of the market share.
prompt: A video-game developer with a few very popular PC games sells them in boxes through retailers and struggles to deliver game updates and to fight cheating. Proposal (2003): require its own new games to run through a mandatory online client that handles updates, anti-cheat checks and purchases, and later open the client as a store for other developers' games. Risks raised: players dislike mandatory online accounts and large downloads; retail partners may drop its boxed games; early bugs in the client; home broadband is not universal; competitors may copy the idea.

evidence_quote: It is the largest email service worldwide, with 1.8 billion users.
prompt: A search company wants to launch a free web email service. Existing free webmail services give each user a few megabytes of storage and users routinely delete old messages. Proposal (2004): launch a free email service with a gigabyte of storage per user, fast search across all mail and a fast web interface, funded by text ads matched to message content, invitation-only at first. Risks raised: storage and server cost of a gigabyte per user; privacy objections to scanning mail for ads; email is a mature market with entrenched incumbents; no direct revenue at launch.

evidence_quote: On November 15, 2007, Microsoft celebrated Xbox Live's 5th anniversary by offering its then over 8 million subscribers the title Carcassonne free of charge
prompt: A software company's new game console, launched in 2001, faces rivals that leave online play free or up to each game's publisher. Proposal (2002): launch a paid, console-wide online service with one shared player identity, a friends list, voice chat and matchmaking for all games, requiring broadband and an annual subscription on top of the console price. Risks raised: few homes have broadband; players expect online play to be free; a mandatory subscription may limit the player base; the service needs hosting and support operations the company has never run.

evidence_quote: over 400,000 units were sold in its first year; the one-millionth Mustang was sold within two years of its launch.
prompt: A large car maker's cheap compact car is reliable but dull. Young buyers from the postwar baby boom are entering the market and want sporty styling at a low price. Proposal (1964): launch a sporty two-door coupe and convertible built on the compact car's mechanical parts, with a long hood and short rear deck, a low base price and a long options list so buyers can customize it, backed by a very large launch advertising campaign. Risks raised: demand for sporty small cars is unproven at volume; sharing parts with a cheap economy car may make it look cheap; heavy launch spending before sales are known.

evidence_quote: The Game Boy and GBC sold an estimated 118.69 million combined.
prompt: A game company that leads the home console market is considering a handheld. A rival handheld with a color screen and stronger hardware exists. Proposal (1989): launch a handheld with a small monochrome screen, a modest processor, long battery life and a retail price of US$89.95, bundled with a puzzle game, backed by a marketing campaign of about US$20 million. Risks raised: a monochrome screen against color rivals; modest hardware specifications; the company's earlier handheld devices each played a single game; thin margins at that price.

evidence_quote: The final 747 was delivered to Atlas Air in January 2023 after a 54-year production run, with 1,574 aircraft built.
prompt: An aircraft maker that dominates the jet airliner market is asked by its largest airline customer to build an aircraft about two and a half times the size of its current jetliner, to cut the airline's cost per seat as air travel grows quickly. Proposal (1966): commit to develop and build a four-engine wide-body jet, with a new factory and a new high-bypass engine from a supplier, designed with a raised cockpit so it can later be converted to a freighter. Risks raised: the development and factory outlay is far larger than any the company has made; the engine is unproven; supersonic airliners are expected to replace subsonic jets; only one airline has ordered so far.

evidence_quote: Apple used NeXT's software technologies as the foundation for Rhapsody, Mac OS X (later macOS), and the operating systems that followed.
prompt: A personal computer maker has a dated operating system, has failed twice to replace it from inside, and its market share is falling. Proposal (1996): buy a small software company that built a modern, object-oriented operating system, for a few hundred million dollars, to use as the core of its replacement operating system, and bring its founder back as an advisor. Risks raised: the acquired company has itself sold few units; migrating existing software and developers to a new core is risky; the founder has a difficult history with the company; the price is high against small revenue; licensing another vendor's system is an alternative.

evidence_quote: In April 2021, Amazon reported that Prime had 200 million subscribers worldwide.
prompt: An online retailer charges per-order shipping fees, which are the biggest friction for repeat customers. Proposal (2005): launch an annual membership at $79 that gives free two-day shipping on all eligible orders and discounted one-day rates. Risks raised: heavy buyers will order more often and shipping costs may exceed fee revenue; the retailer takes a large short-term margin hit; the offer is hard to reverse once customers hold memberships; the economics are unproven.

evidence_quote: By launching its Intel Inside marketing campaign in 1991, Intel was able to associate brand loyalty with consumer selection, so that by the end of the 1990s, its line of Pentium processors had become a household name.
prompt: A leading chip maker sells microprocessors only to computer makers, buyers do not know which chip is in their computer, and clone makers use similar part numbers. Proposal (1991): launch a consumer brand campaign with a logo and a program that pays part of computer makers' advertising costs when their ads carry the logo, to make buyers ask for its chip by name. Risks raised: consumer advertising for a component is unprecedented; the program takes a large share of the marketing budget; computer makers may resent being told how to advertise; benefits may not show in sales.

evidence_quote: Including the DS Lite and DSi models, the Nintendo DS has sold 154 million units, becoming the best-selling Nintendo console until it was surpassed by the Nintendo Switch in 2025.
prompt: A game company that dominates handheld gaming faces a rival's well-funded handheld with stronger graphics and media features. Proposal (2004): launch a handheld with two screens, one of them touch-sensitive, instead of matching the rival's hardware, aimed at broadening the audience beyond core players, at a lower price than the rival, while keeping its older handheld on sale. Risks raised: unusual hardware may confuse developers; the rival has stronger graphics; touch-screen games are unproven; two screens add cost; it may be dismissed as a gimmick.

evidence_quote: In June 2011, Specific Media Group and Justin Timberlake jointly purchased the company for approximately $35 million.
prompt: A global media conglomerate wants a social-media presence. A fast-growing social network site is for sale; it has little revenue and is built on pages that users customize. Proposal (2005): buy it for about $580 million, keep it as a separate unit, and sell advertising across the conglomerate's channels. Risks raised: a large price for a site with modest revenue; a college-focused rival network has begun to grow; user-generated pages create brand-safety issues; a young audience is hard to monetize; the site's technology was built quickly and unevenly.

evidence_quote: After only 48 days on the market, Microsoft discontinued the Kin line on June 30, 2010
prompt: A software company wants to enter smartphones aimed at teenagers who live on social networks, after buying a maker of a popular messaging phone. Proposal (2010): launch two social-networking phones on a new in-house operating system, sold through a single carrier with a mandatory monthly data plan, with no application store at launch. Risks raised: rival smartphones already have large app catalogs; the data plan costs about as much as a full smartphone plan, which is high for teenagers; the phones use a new operating system rather than the company's own mobile platform; two years of development are already sunk.

evidence_quote: On August 18, 2011, 49 days after the TouchPad was launched in the United States, HP announced that it would discontinue all current devices running webOS.
prompt: A computer maker bought a mobile-operating-system company a year ago and now has a tablet ready. Proposal (2011): launch a tablet on the acquired operating system, priced in line with the market-leading tablet, with a small app catalog, and invest heavily in developer outreach and advertising. Risks raised: the market leader dominates tablets; the app catalog is a small fraction of the leader's; the operating system has almost no market share; the company's leadership is in transition; shoppers see the product as unproven.

evidence_quote: On January 15, 2015, Google announced that it would stop producing the Google Glass prototype.
prompt: A search and advertising company's research lab has a head-worn display with a camera, voice control and a small screen. Proposal (2013): sell it to early adopters in an invitation-only program at $1,500, then to the general public, positioned as an everyday consumer product. Risks raised: privacy objections to a wearable camera; a high price; no clear everyday use for most people; social acceptance of wearing it in public; short battery life.

evidence_quote: After much public outcry, the company reverted to its previous "blue box" logo on October 11, after less than a week in use.
prompt: A mature clothing retailer wants to look more contemporary. Its logo, white capital letters in a dark blue square, has been used for decades. Proposal (2010): replace it with a plain neutral-typeface wordmark and a small blue square, rolled out to every channel at once with no advance announcement. Risks raised: loyal customers are attached to the old logo; social media makes backlash instant; the old square is what the brand is recognized by; the new design was not tested with customers.

evidence_quote: After two months of negative consumer reaction and a 20% drop in sales, Tropicana switched back to its original design of an orange skewered by a drinking straw.
prompt: The leading chilled orange-juice brand has printed a picture of an orange with a drinking straw in it on its carton for years. Proposal (2009): replace the cartons nationwide with a minimalist design showing a glass of juice, a cap shaped like an orange and a vertically rotated brand name, keeping the same recipe and price, launched in all stores at once with a large advertising campaign. Risks raised: the old image is the brand's main shelf cue; shoppers may fail to recognize the carton; the redesign is costly; the buyer base is loyal and older.

evidence_quote: It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 15, 2018, and sold its assets to ESL Investments in 2019.
prompt: A discount-store chain that recently emerged from court-supervised restructuring has weak sales. It proposes to buy a larger, older department-store and appliance chain whose sales are also declining. Proposal (2004): acquire it, close the deal in 2005, merge corporate functions, convert some stores to the combined format, and sell the older chain's brands in the discount stores. Risks raised: both chains have declining sales; stores are old and underinvested; cost savings are uncertain; the two chains' customers differ; big-box rivals are growing.

evidence_quote: By late 1993, Crystal Pepsi was discontinued, and the final batches were delivered to retailers during the first few months of 1994.
prompt: The second-largest cola maker faces slowing soft-drink growth. Test markets for a clear cola, positioned as a purer alternative, drew a positive response. Proposal (1992): launch it nationwide with a large marketing campaign as a major brand extension. Risks raised: shoppers may link cola flavor with color; novelty buyers may not repeat; it may cannibalize the flagship; test markets can overstate demand; rivals may launch copies.

evidence_quote: Pets.com stock had fallen from its IPO price of $11 per share in February 2000 to $0.19 the day of its liquidation announcement.
prompt: An online pet-supplies start-up has grown quickly on venture funding. Proposal (early 2000): go public, use the proceeds for a national television advertising campaign including a major sports broadcast, buy its largest online competitor, and build more warehouses, while selling many products below what the company pays for them to win customers. Risks raised: heavy, low-margin goods are costly to ship; negative gross margins on many items; high customer-acquisition cost; capital markets could close; competitors are also spending heavily.

evidence_quote: The Zune had failed to capture significant market share after five years against the Apple iPod
prompt: A software company wants to compete with the dominant digital music player. Proposal (2006): launch its own music player and a music store and subscription, with wireless song sharing between players, a larger screen and a new desktop client, backed by a large marketing budget. Risks raised: the leader holds an enormous share and a loyal ecosystem; the new device and store drop the copy-protection standard that the company had promoted to partner stores and device makers; the company is late to market; labels may restrict sharing; there is no clear price advantage.

evidence_quote: Despite having the largest advertising and promotional budget in fast food history at the time, it was soon discontinued after failing to become popular.
prompt: A fast-food chain with a child-centered image wants to grow among adults. Proposal (1996): launch a premium burger aimed at adults, priced above the core menu, supported by the largest advertising and promotional budget the industry has seen. Risks raised: customers come for kids' meals and value, not premium food; adults see the chain as fast, not premium; the higher price may deter regular buyers; heavy spending before demand is shown.

evidence_quote: After a poorly received redesign in 2010, its audience plummeted and much of its user base migrated to its competitor Reddit.
prompt: A social news site, where users vote stories to the front page, has a loyal community but slowing traffic. Proposal (2010): rewrite the product from scratch as a new version with a redesigned front page that changes how stories surface and favors publishers' content, and move all users to it at once. Risks raised: the core community values the existing voting mechanics; a full rewrite is a large engineering risk; a launch to all users at once leaves no rollback; a rival community site is growing.
